name: Portuguese Angola
info: Portugal's colony on the Atlantic coast of west-central Africa, founded at Luanda in 1575, for two centuries a great slave-trading enterprise tied to Brazil, and independent as Angola in 1975.

facts.capital: Luanda (São Paulo de Luanda; held by the Dutch as Fort Aardenburgh, 1640–1648)
facts.founder: Paulo Dias de Novais, who founded Luanda in 1575
facts.predecessor: The Kingdom of Kongo and the Kingdom of Ndongo; other polities of the region such as the Kingdom of Lunda, the Mbunda Kingdom, Bié and Bailundo
facts.successor: The People's Republic of Angola (11 November 1975)

t: Between 1580 and the 1820s well over a million people from present-day Angola were shipped as slaves to the New World, mainly to Brazil, and Oliver and Atmore called the colony 'a gigantic slave-trading enterprise' for 200 years.

Portugal ruled only the coast in the 16th and 17th centuries; full control of the territory came at the beginning of the 20th century, through wars of conquest and agreements with other European powers.
Forced labour lasted until 1962, and the war for independence that began in 1961 ended only after the Carnation Revolution in Lisbon, with independence on 11 November 1975.
dyk: From 1640 to 1648 Luanda was Dutch, ruled as Fort Aardenburgh: the Dutch, who had seized north-eastern Brazil, wanted slaves for its sugarcane plantations.
ev: Paulo Dias de Novais founds the settlement of São Paulo de Loanda, Luanda, on the coast south of the Kingdom of Kongo
The Dutch hold Luanda as Fort Aardenburgh until Portugal re-establishes its authority
Portugal defeats the Kingdom of Kongo at the Battle of Mbwila, but suffers a disastrous defeat at the Battle of Kitombo when it invades Kongo in 1670
The slave trade is abolished, badly damaging the colony's economy; Angola's ports are opened to legal foreign shipping in 1844
Agreements with the Congo Free State, the German Empire and France fix most of the colony's borders
General António Júlio da Costa Pereira de Eça's campaign reoccupies southern Angola after the German-backed Ovambo Uprising
Holden Roberto's incursion of 15 March opens the war for independence; the same year the Estatuto do Indigenato is abolished
On 11 November Angola becomes a sovereign state under the Alvor Agreement, as the People's Republic of Angola

sections.foundation:
Portuguese presence began with the explorer Diogo Cão, who reached the Kongo Kingdom in 1484. The land was then home to a number of separate peoples, some organised as kingdoms or federations. The Portuguese, interested above all in the slave trade, kept a peaceful and profitable relationship with the Kongo's rulers and nobles; kings such as João I and Afonso I studied Christianity, learned Portuguese and shared the profits of the trade. The Portuguese set up small trading posts on the lower Congo and a more important settlement at Soyo, and from the start their expeditions aimed at the conversion of the peoples they met, as they had since the conquest of Ceuta in 1415.

In 1575 Paulo Dias de Novais founded São Paulo de Loanda, Luanda, on the coast south of the Kongo Kingdom; Benguela followed in the 17th century, and the town of Mbaka was founded in 1618. For two centuries Portugal held the coast and fought the kingdoms inland. A mestiço elite emerged in Luanda by the early 17th century, its wealth drawn from buying captives from the interior, and the Afro-Portuguese communities called 'Ambaquista' grew where the colony reached inland. Portugal annexed what remained of the Kingdom of Ndongo after the Battle of Pungo Andongo, and in the 18th century gained control of most of the central highlands.
sections.socioeconomy:
Between 1580 and the 1820s well over a million people were shipped from present-day Angola as slaves, mainly to Brazil. Most were captured by other Africans in wars and raids, with Imbangala and Mbundu slave hunters, and sold to Luanda's merchants; Brazilian ships were the most numerous in Luanda and Benguela, so that Angola was in effect a colony of Brazil. From 1764 the economy slowly shifted to production for home use and export; the slave trade was abolished in 1836, ruining the mestiço elite, and by 1850 Luanda exported palm and peanut oil, wax, ivory, cotton, coffee and cocoa.

From 1908 a 'native tax' pushed Africans into the money economy. Forced labour took many forms, the harshest shipping workers to São Tomé and Príncipe, from which few returned; in 1954 over 300,000 Angolans were estimated to work under forced labour, which was abolished only in 1962. Edward Ross, reporting to the League of Nations in 1924, called the system 'virtually state serfdom'. Diamonds were found in Lunda in 1912, and Diamang, granted the concession in 1917, became the largest commercial operator, its wealth made by African labourers, many forcibly recruited. Iron ore was mined from the mid-1950s, petroleum was found in 1955, and in 1973 oil overtook coffee as the largest export.
sections.military:
Angola was governed in a highly militaristic style. The Portuguese Army generally kept about 2,000 European soldiers there from the 16th century into the 20th, backed by the guerra preta ('black war') of 5,000 to 20,000 African troops raised by loyal sobas. Service was unpopular: most soldiers were degredados, convicts sent to ease prison overcrowding, deserters and adventurers, and only in the final campaigns of conquest of 1890 to 1920 were first-rate officers posted there regularly. Portugal defeated the Kongo Kingdom at the Battle of Mbwila on 29 October 1665, but was disastrously defeated at the Battle of Kitombo in 1670.

The Campaigns of Pacification and Occupation began in 1838, and Viye was annexed in 1890. In the First World War German forces from South West Africa took Naulila in December 1914, and several peoples revolted, among them the German-backed Ovambo Uprising of King Mandume ya Ndemufayo of Oukwanyama. In March 1915 about 10,000 troops under General António Júlio da Costa Pereira de Eça reoccupied the south, massacring the population, burning villages and deepening a famine; a 2026 study described the campaign as genocide. Between 1939 and 1943 army operations against the Mucubal killed hundreds and sent 3,529 prisoners to concentration camps.
sections.governance:
Every Captain-General, renamed Governor-General in 1836, was a serving army or naval officer. E. Silva Correia wrote in 1782 that in no part of the Portuguese world was an army more necessary than in Angola, and Governor Calheiros e Menezes in 1867 that 'the normal condition of the administration of this colony is to make war'. In the 20th century Angola was ruled by the Estado Novo regime. In 1951 it became an overseas province, legally as much a part of Portugal as Lisbon; government was highly centralised, with authority running from the Prime Minister's office in Lisbon down a rigid chain of command, and nearly all officials came from Portugal.

The governor-general, appointed by the Portuguese cabinet on the Overseas Minister's recommendation, held both executive and legislative authority, advised by a Government Council and served by five secretaries; a Legislative Council of limited powers approved the budget, and an Economic and Social Council had to be consulted on all draft legislation. From 1967 Angola sent delegates to the National Assembly. The Organic Law of June 1972 made Angola an autonomous state, the 'State of Angola' from 1 January 1973, with Portugal keeping defence and foreign relations, and elections for a legislative assembly were held in 1973; but the changes were extremely limited and the new government was the old provincial one under other titles.
sections.impact:
For two centuries Angola was bound to Brazil by the Atlantic slave trade and its middle passage, and Jesuit missions carried Brazilian influence in religion and education. Portugal subjugated the neighbouring states of the highlands, among them Bié and Bailundo, one by one. The borders of present-day Angola were drawn by agreements with the Congo Free State, the German Empire and France in 1885–1886, the Anglo-Portuguese Treaty of 1891 and the arbitration of King Victor Emmanuel III in 1905; the Treaty of Simulambuco of 1885 made Cabinda a protectorate, later joined to the colony. The territory covered 1,246,700 square kilometres.

After 1951 the Estado Novo encouraged mass settlement: settlers numbered 80,000 in 1950 and 335,000 by 1974, the second largest white population in Africa after South Africa, and they owned almost all businesses and coffee plantations. Society in the 1950s was described as one of 'extreme racism', with whites at the top, mestiços below them, then assimilados, and the unassimilated African majority at the bottom; settlers' children had schools while Africans had almost none. Education for Africans widened from the 1950s, and the Estudos Gerais Universitários de Angola, founded in 1962, became the University of Luanda in 1968.
sections.decline:
The settlers' boom, and the regime's open favour to them, angered the African population. In the late 1950s the FNLA and the MPLA organised against Portuguese rule and forced labour. On 15 March 1961 Holden Roberto led 4,000 to 5,000 militants into the north, killing at least 1,000 whites and an unknown number of blacks; Portugal abolished the Estatuto do Indigenato that September and sent thousands of troops. The guerrillas were divided by ethnicity, ideology and leadership: the MPLA drew on the Mbundu, mestiços and Luanda, the FNLA on the Bakongo, and UNITA, founded by Jonas Savimbi in 1966, on the Ovimbundu. The MPLA's push into the east from 1966 was driven back by the Portuguese campaign of 1971, but the movements were never fully defeated.

The long colonial war, international sanctions and its cost at home led to the mutiny of Portuguese officers in the Carnation Revolution of 25 April 1974, which overthrew the regime of Marcelo Caetano; in May the new junta proclaimed a truce with the guerrillas. Hundreds of thousands of Portuguese citizens, the retornados, left as refugees. On 11 November 1975 Angola became a sovereign state under the Alvor Agreement, as the People's Republic of Angola, which re-annexed the short-lived Republic of Cabinda.

summary: Portuguese Angola began as the coastal settlement of Luanda in 1575 and for two centuries was chiefly a slave-trading colony tied to Brazil. Conquered inland only by the early 20th century and worked by forced labour until 1962, it was settled heavily after 1951, fought a war for independence from 1961 and became independent in 1975.
references: Douglas L. Wheeler, 'The Portuguese Army in Angola', The Journal of Modern African Studies (1969)
Thomas H. Henriksen, 'People's Wars in Angola, Mozambique, and Guinea-Bissau', The Journal of Modern African Studies (1976)
Geoffrey Wright, The Destruction of a Nation: United States' Policy Towards Angola Since 1945 (Pluto Press, 1997)
Fernando Tavares Pimenta, 'White Settler Politics and Euro-African Nationalism in Angola, 1945-1975', in The Routledge Handbook of the History of Settler Colonialism (Routledge, 2016)
Lisa Åkesson, Postcolonial Portuguese Migration to Angola: Migrants Or Masters? (Springer International Publishing, 2018)

pointDescs.1575: Paulo Dias de Novais founds Luanda on the coast south of the Kingdom of Kongo; the slave trade with Brazil soon becomes the colony's business.
pointDescs.1618: The town of Mbaka is founded inland, giving its name to the Afro-Portuguese Ambaquista communities.
pointDescs.1640: During the Iberian Union the Dutch seize Luanda and rule it as Fort Aardenburgh, seeking slaves for the sugar plantations of north-eastern Brazil.
pointDescs.1648: Dutch rule of Luanda ends and Portugal re-establishes its authority.
pointDescs.1665: Portugal defeats the Kingdom of Kongo at the Battle of Mbwila on 29 October.
pointDescs.1670: A Portuguese invasion of Kongo ends in disastrous defeat at the Battle of Kitombo.
pointDescs.1764: A gradual change begins from a slave-based society to one producing for home consumption and export; Portugal has gained most of the central highlands in this century.
pointDescs.1836: The slave trade is abolished, badly damaging the economy and ruining the mestiço elite that lived by it; the Captain-General is renamed Governor-General.
pointDescs.1844: Angola's ports are opened to legal foreign shipping; by 1850 Luanda is among the most developed cities of the empire outside Portugal.
pointDescs.1885: Agreements with the Congo Free State, Germany and France fix most borders, and the Treaty of Simulambuco makes Cabinda a protectorate.
pointDescs.1890: Viye is annexed in the Campaigns of Pacification and Occupation; the final campaigns of conquest run to 1920.
pointDescs.1914: German forces from South West Africa take Naulila in December and drive the Portuguese from the Humbe region; peoples of the south revolt.
pointDescs.1915: Some 10,000 troops under Pereira de Eça reoccupy the south, massacring the population and deepening a famine.
pointDescs.1917: Diamang is granted the diamond concession and becomes the colony's largest commercial operator, on the labour of many forcibly recruited Africans.
pointDescs.1951: Angola becomes an overseas province of Portugal, and the Estado Novo begins to encourage mass Portuguese settlement.
pointDescs.1961: Holden Roberto's incursion opens the war for independence; Portugal sends thousands of troops and abolishes the Estatuto do Indigenato.
pointDescs.1971: The Portuguese campaign on the Eastern Front drives the guerrilla movements beyond Angola's borders.
pointDescs.1973: Angola becomes the 'State of Angola'; oil overtakes coffee as the largest export, and settlers number over 300,000.
pointDescs.1974: The Carnation Revolution of 25 April overthrows the Estado Novo; in May the new junta proclaims a truce with the guerrillas, and the retornados begin to leave.
pointDescs.1975: On 11 November Angola becomes independent under the Alvor Agreement as the People's Republic of Angola.

notes: The article's 'Brazilian Highlands, Planalto' for the home of Bié and Bailundo is evidently the Angolan planalto; the profile says only 'the highlands'.
The Battle of Pungo Andongo and the conquest of the central highlands are undated in the article and are given without years. The 1764 point carries the 18th-century gain of the highlands.

The 1971 Eastern Front section and the 1972 Development Plan are written from the Portuguese side ('hearts and minds', 'effectively won'); the profile keeps only the campaign's outcome and the article's own statement that the movements were never fully defeated.
The genocide description of the 1915 campaign is attributed to 'a 2026 study' as in the article, which names no author.

The article gives settler figures that do not quite agree (335,000 settlers in 1974; 400,000 European residents in 1974 excluding soldiers; 324,000 in 1973); the profile uses 80,000 (1950) and 335,000 (1974).
Henriksen and Wheeler are journal articles (the guide asks for works; they are among the article's bibliography). Chabal's article and the Portuguese reference works are not listed.
